documentation.range: Atractosteus spatula global range is estimated to cover 200,000-2,500,000 square km (Hammerson, 2004). Historical range included the Mississippi River basin in the USA, from southwestern Ohio (Trautman 1981), southern Indiana, and southern Illinois (Smith 1979) to the Gulf of Mexico; also the Gulf Coastal Plain from the Florida panhandle (Gilbert 1992) to Veracruz, Mexico, with disjunct occurrences in Nicaragua and northwestern Costa Rica (Lee et al. 1980). Now the species is extirpated or very rare in most of the northern part of its range north of the Gulf Coastal Plain (Hammerson, 2004).
documentation.population: Total population size is unknown but presumably exceeds 10,000 to > 1,000,000 individuals (Hammerson, 2004). Atractosteus spatula is uncommon to rare throughout most of the range, except locally in swamps and bayous of the south-central United States (Page & Burr 2011) and the brackish waters of the Gulf of Mexico where it is frequently seen (Hoese & Moore, 1998). Area of occupancy and abundance have declined over the long term, particularly in the northern part of the range. The degree of decline is uncertain but likely exceeds 30 percent (Hammerson, 2004).
documentation.habitats: This gar is one of the largest freshwater fishes in North America, attaining sizes of up to 3 m and 300 pounds. Eats mostly fishes and crabs and occasionally other small vertebrates. Habitat includes sluggish pools of large rivers and their bayous, oxbow lakes, swamps, and backwaters, brackish and marine waters along the coast (Page & Burr 2011).
documentation.threats:
This species is known to destroy gillnets and trawls in both freshwater and estuarine habitats (O'Connell et al. 2007). As a result, fishing pressure, habitat alteration, and active management to remove all gar species as nuisance fishes has reduced A. spatula populations throughout its range, including Oklahoma, Texas, Alabama, Mississippi, and Florida (Gilbert 1992, Scarnecchia 1992, Ross et al. 2001, Aguilera et al. 2002).

This species is threatened by habitat loss and degradation from urban and agricultural runoff, shell dredging, over-fishing, artificial saltwater and freshwater inputs, shoreline alteration, and industrial discharges (O'Connell et al. 2007). Factors such as fragmentation of river-floodplain corridors, impoundments, channelisation and urbanisation have likely impacted Atractosteus spatula populations, especially as the population of Texas expands and water demands increase, reducing connectivity of river channels to backwater spawning and nursery areas, and affect estuarine habitats by increasing salinity (Buckmeier, 2008).
The species is also threatened by recreational and commercial fishing in parts of its range (Garcia de Leon et al. 2001; Aguilera et al. 2002).
Natural introgression with sympatric Lepisosteus osseus and L. oculatus may threaten this species, especially in areas with depressed population abundances (Bohn et al. 2017).
documentation.measures:
In recent years management efforts have changed from attempts to limit or exterminate gar populations to conserving whole aquatic ecosystems, and there is also growing interest to manage Atractosteus spatula as both a game species (e.g., bow hunting in particular; Ross et al. 2001) and a commercial species (Garcia de Leon et al. 2001).

There are also some preliminary attempts to examine the possibility of culturing Atractosteus spatula as an aquaculture species or at least to use hatchery techniques to augment declining natural populations (Aguilera et al. 2002).
documentation.use_trade: Common as a market fish in Louisiana and numerous enough to support a gillnet fishery in a reservoir in Tamualipas, Mexico (Garcia de Leon et al. 2001).
documentation.rationale: Atractosteus spatula has a large distribution from central and southeastern United States to eastern Mexico, Nicaragua and northwestern Costa Rica. The species is uncommon to rare in most of its range but abundant enough to support fisheries in some areas. Local population declines have been observed as a result of overfishing, habitat degradation from river channelization and impoundments, loss of spawning habitat and loss of passages between main river channels and floodplains.While it is declining in parts of its range, it is not thought that any global population decline is likely to meet (or be close to meeting) the threshold for Vulnerable. Therefore the species is assessed as Least Concern.
